paper.title: Cell adhesion molecule-related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog-producing cells.
paper.abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.
paper.full_text:
INTRODUCTION
Embryonic tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis depend on temporally and spatially controlled intercellular signals that are conveyed through morphogens and growth factors. Morphogens act in time- and concentration-dependent manners to govern cell fate, and growth factors signal at short and long distance to instruct cellular growth, division, and differentiation (1). Dysregulation of morphogen or growth factor–regulated pathways can trigger developmental disorders or cancers, underscoring the importance of tight control of signal deployment, reception, and interpretation during tissue development and maintenance (2–6).

One mechanism by which cells precisely control delivery of crucial information is by extending dedicated transport filopodia called cytonemes. These structures are actin-based, long, thin, and dynamic, and can originate from both signal-producing and -receiving cells (7, 8). Cytonemes have been observed during tissue development and in the organization and maintenance of stem cell niches in Drosophila, zebrafish, chick, axolotl, and mammalian model systems (9–15). Cell-based assays suggest that human cells also form cytonemes, supporting broadly conserved use of the specialized signaling filopodia (16).

Components of Hedgehog (Hh)/Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), Wingless (Wg)/WNT, bone morphogenic protein (BMP)/Decapentaplegic (Dpp), Notch, and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling pathways can be transported along cytonemes across a range of cellular contexts (7, 10, 11, 13, 17–21). As facilitators of long-range signaling in developing and expanding tissues, cytonemes often extend to great lengths to reach their intended cellular targets (7, 14). In stem cell niches, cytoneme signaling promotes self-reinforcing regulatory activity and also provides positional information that dictates differentiation and de-differentiation for niche organization (19, 22). This highlights their ability to adapt their function for context-dependent needs.

Cytoneme biogenesis and cargo specificity are tightly controlled such that individual extensions typically restrict themselves to transport of one type of signaling protein or receptor at a time (10, 23–25). For example, during wing disc development in Drosophila, cells of the air sac primordium (ASP) extend spatially distinct cytonemes that either contain the FGF receptor Branchless (Bnl) or the Dpp receptor Thickveins (Tkv) (23). Similarly, wing disc-localized myoblasts form dedicated cytonemes that either transport the Notch ligand Delta to the ASP or receive Wg from the wing disc (24). In NIH3T3 cells, expression of SHH, WNT, FGF2, or the Notch ligand Jagged-1 correlates with increased cytoneme occurrence rates (26), suggesting that cargo-specific signals linked to either ligand production or autocrine activity might induce cytoneme formation. Consistent with this hypothesis, published reports indicate that cargo proteins must communicate with actin regulators for increased cytoneme biogenesis to occur (11, 27–29). A knowledge gap remains in understanding of how such factors are recruited in pathway-specific manners to sites of cytoneme initiation.

Studies focused on WNT and SHH cytonemes have begun to close this knowledge gap by revealing that distinct transmembrane ligand-binding proteins can enhance cytoneme formation. WNT8a functions with its co-receptor receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor 2 (ROR2) and the planar cell polarity protein Vangl2 to promote cytoneme elongation in a Cdc42, N-WASP, and I-BAR protein (IRSp53)–dependent manner (8, 28, 29). Similarly, the SHH-binding, immunoglobulin super family molecules Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) and Brother of CDON (BOC) have been shown to localize to cytonemes and promote their formation (26, 30). Overexpression of either protein drives ectopic cytoneme occurrence in the absence of SHH, and their combined removal prevents SHH-mediated cytoneme enhancement (26).

The Drosophila ortholog of CDON, interference hedgehog (Ihog), can stabilize Hh cytonemes when overexpressed (17, 31). This activity is dependent on the Ihog fibronectin (FNIII) domains, which engage in trans homophilic interactions that link cytonemes along their lengths (32). Ihog has also been shown to bind glypicans in the extracellular milieu to guide and support cytonemes as they elongate (32, 33). The intracellular domain of Ihog recruits the actin cross-linker Cheerio (filamin A), suggesting that the co-receptor can stabilize cytonemes through both extracellular and intracellular interactions (34). Whereas adhesion/homophilic activity by the BOC and CDON extracellular domains (ECDs) has not yet been demonstrated, the adhesion properties of Ihog suggest that they may be capable of cell adhesion molecule (CAM)–like activity in SHH cytonemes.

The ability of BOC and CDON to influence SHH cytoneme dynamics is notable because they were first proposed to function in SHH-receiving cells as co-receptors, directly binding to both SHH and its receptor Patched (PTCH) to facilitate pathway activation (35, 36). Subsequent models indicated that BOC and CDON cooperate with a third, GPI-linked, co-receptor, growth arrest specific 1 (GAS1), whereby BOC and CDON cluster ligand on the cell surface and GAS1 transfers it to PTCH for pathway activation (37, 38). As such, the discovery of their ability to promote cytoneme occurrence suggests context-specific diversification of their function in the SHH signaling pathway.

SHH deployment from ligand-producing cells requires Dispatched 1 (DISP), a 12-pass transmembrane protein that is structurally related to PTCH (39–41). DISP promotes transport of SHH through at least two mechanisms: (i) by transferring it to the secreted glycoprotein SCUBE2, which is reported to function as an extracellular SHH chaperone, and (ii) by enhancing SHH loading into cytonemes for protrusion-based transport (10, 42, 43). DISP can also bind BOC and CDON in SHH-producing cells where it colocalizes with them at distinct puncta along SHH-transporting cytonemes (26, 30). This suggests that BOC and/or CDON associate with SHH-bound DISP in ligand-producing cells to form an SHH deployment complex (SDC).

Herein, we interrogate the function of the SDC in vitro and in vivo and map a signaling cascade that is activated by BOC or CDON to facilitate SHH cytoneme elongation. This BOC/CDON-initiated signal instructs cytoneme growth from the ligand source cells through recruitment of the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) FERM, RhoGEF, and Pleckstrin domain-containing protein 1 (FARP1) for Cdc42 activation. This activity is distinct from the well-established receiving cell signaling mechanism by which BOC and CDON promote activation of the signal transducing protein Smoothened (SMO) in SHH-stimulated cells through their function in the PTCH co-receptor complex (35, 36, 38). Live imaging of murine neural tubes reveals that in vivo loss of Cdon specifically in SHH-producing neuroepithelial cells reduces cytoneme length and extension frequency and results in altered specification of ventral neural progenitor cell populations. Altogether, the results presented here support a crucial role for SHH binding, CAM-related proteins as conduits for actin organization into cytonemes that ensure morphogen gradient precision.

SHH induces cytoneme formation through BOC and CDON
DISP and PTCH are 12-pass transmembrane proteins that bind SHH in signal-producing and -receiving cells, respectively. DISP is required for SHH release from ligand-producing cells while PTCH receives SHH ligand for pathway activation (44–46). We previously showed that Disp1−/− mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (44) and Ptch1−/− MEFs (47) are still capable of forming SHH-induced cytonemes (26). However, because these receptors are structurally similar and both able to bind SHH, we sought to test whether DISP and PTCH are compensating for one another in the single knockout cell lines. We used CRISPR-Cas9 on Disp1−/− MEFs (44) to generate Disp1/Ptch1/Ptch2 triple knockout (TKO) MEFs, enabling direct comparison of the cell lines (fig. S1A). Knockout lines generated in this study were validated by testing for expression of the targeted gene and by functional assays, as appropriate (fig. S1, B to G). We evaluated the cytoneme-forming potential of Disp1/Ptch1/Ptch2−/− MEFs following expression of SHH by quantifying the percentage of cells extending cytonemes in control and ligand-stimulated populations. We considered a cellular extension to be a cytoneme if it was thin (∼200 nm), was ≥10 μm in length, appeared to be closed ended, and, in assays with fluorescently tagged ligand, contained SHH (48). Consistent with our previous report (26), the single gene knockout cell lines remained responsive to SHH expression, increasing cytoneme occurrence similar to wild-type (WT) control MEFs. Similarly, Disp1/Ptch1/Ptch2−/− TKO MEFs maintained the ability to increase cytoneme occurrence rates in response to SHH expression (Fig. 1A). These results confirm that neither PTCH nor DISP is required for cytoneme outgrowth from SHH-producing cells.

To evaluate the requirement of additional SDC components for initiation of SHH cytonemes, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to generate Boc/Disp1−/− double knockout (DKO), Cdon/Disp1−/− DKO, and Boc/Cdon/Disp1−/− TKO MEFs (fig. S1, A and C) from Disp1−/− cells (44). Loss of BOC or CDON individually or in combination on the Disp1−/− background reduced SHH cytoneme induction (Fig. 1B). To test whether expression of exogenous BOC or CDON could rescue cytoneme occurrence rates in the knockout cells, we expressed GFP control or GFP-tagged BOC or CDON proteins in SHH-expressing knockout cells and then quantified cytoneme occurrence. Individual overexpression of either BOC or CDON restored cytoneme outgrowth in SHH-expressing knockout lines (Fig. 1C, gray columns). Whereas combined loss of either Boc or Cdon with Disp1 disrupted the ability of SHH to induce cytonemes in the DKO lines, individual add back of either BOC or CDON was sufficient to rescue cytoneme occurrence rates in Boc/Cdon/Disp1−/− TKO MEFs (Fig. 1B compared to Fig. 1C, black columns). This suggests a requirement for both CAM-related proteins to form a functional SDC for cytoneme outgrowth when they are expressed at endogenous levels in the absence of Disp1, but that when overexpressed, either BOC or CDON can compensate for loss of the other SDC components to drive cytoneme formation (Fig. 1C). Nonetheless, these results support that either BOC or CDON is required for the SDC to promote cytoneme biogenesis.

Given our observations that BOC and CDON promote cytoneme occurrence in SHH-expressing cells (Fig. 1) (10, 26), we sought to specifically evaluate how their expression domains overlapped with cytoneme-producing cell populations in vivo. Thus, we performed RNAscope in situ hybridization (ISH) analysis on mouse embryonic neural tubes at E8.5 (10 somites), E9.5 (24 somites), and E10.5 (fig. S2A). Consistent with previous reports, Boc was broadly expressed in the neural tube, detectable in dorsal and intermediate cell populations at each time point evaluated (fig. S2A) (37, 49). Cdon expression was more restricted, localizing to SHH-producing cell populations of the ventral neural tube including the notochord (E8.5 to E10.5) and floor plate (E9.5 to E10.5) (fig. S2A). Consistent with their documented contributions to neural crest migration in zebrafish (49, 50), both Boc and Cdon were expressed in cells surrounding the dorsal roof plate at all time points evaluated, with Cdon expression being particularly intense near the roof plate at E10.5 (fig. S2A). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) of E9.5 neural tubes revealed that protein expression matched gene expression patterns for both BOC and CDON (fig. S2B).

The expression domains of Boc and Cdon were noteworthy to us for two reasons: (i) Floor plate and notochord-localized cells extend SHH-positive cytonemes that contact ventral cell populations, and (ii) cells of the roof plate, which produce WNT1/3a, extend actin-positive protrusions ventrally (10). We therefore hypothesized that, in addition to influencing SHH cytonemes, BOC and CDON might also contribute to formation of WNT-transporting cytonemes. To test whether WNT-stimulated cytoneme occurrence was dependent on BOC or CDON, we expressed WNT1 in WT MEFs or MEFs lacking all three known SHH co-receptors—Boc, Cdon, and Gas1 (26, 51)—and then scored cytoneme occurrence rates in control and ligand-expressing cells. Because GAS1 does not influence cytoneme formation (26), we reasoned that any changes in protrusion occurrence in SHH or WNT-expressing Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− TKO cells would result from loss of BOC and/or CDON. Whereas the ability of SHH to induce cytonemes was attenuated by BOC and CDON loss, WNT1 increased cytoneme occurrence rates similarly in both WT cells and Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− TKO MEFs (fig. S2C). This suggests that the requirement for BOC or CDON for cytoneme regulation may be specific to SHH-containing cytonemes.

CDON is required for SHH cytoneme biogenesis in the murine neural tube
Given its restricted expression domain and apparent specificity to SHH cytonemes, we next sought to determine whether CDON contributes to cytoneme biogenesis or elongation from cells of the embryonic notochord or neural tube floor plate. To do so, we performed live imaging of neural tube sections from Shh-Cre;membrane-Tomato/membrane-GFP (mTmG) reporter mice, which GFP labels membranes of Shh-expressing cells of the developing embryo (9, 10). E9.5 embryos were collected and subjected to gentle vibratome sectioning, and then ventral neural tube sections were immediately imaged using live confocal fluorescence microscopy (Fig. 2A). Over the course of 10 min, numerous thin, GFP-positive, dynamic cellular protrusions were observed extending from cells of the ventral floor plate and reaching toward neighboring non–GFP-labeled cells (Fig. 2B, arrowheads, and movies S1 and S2). To determine whether these extensions were dependent on BOC or CDON, we introduced Boc knockout and Cdon flox alleles into Shh-Cre;mTmG reporter mice (52–54). This allowed generation of animals with conditional deletion of Cdon in Shh-Cre–expressing cells, with or without Boc knockout.

We confirmed specificity of the Cre deletion by evaluating neural tubes of control and experimental embryos using RNAscope and IHC analyses (fig. S2, D and E). Consistent with Cre activity being restricted to Shh-expressing cell populations, Cdon transcript was present in the dorsal neural tube and specifically reduced in the notochord and floor plate of Shh-Cre;Cdonfl/fl E9.5 embryos when compared to Cre-negative controls (fig. S2D, arrowhead). Despite some residual Cdon transcript in ventral-most cells of these neural tubes, likely due to Cre not being expressed until Shh promoter activity is induced in the floor plate around E9.0 (55), CDON protein was nearly undetectable in the ventral neural tube at E9.5. CDON protein levels remained high in the dorsal neural tube, further supporting specificity of Cre activity to Shh-expressing cells (fig. S2E).

Using this validated system, we analyzed cytoneme dynamics in Shh-Cre;mTmG;Boc+/−;Cdonfl/+, Shh-Cre;mTmG;Boc−/−;Cdonfl/+, Shh-Cre;mTmG;Boc+/−;Cdonfl/fl, and Shh-Cre;mTmG;Boc−/−;Cdonfl/fl embryos (Fig. 2C and movies S3 and S4). Cytoneme behavior was evaluated by scoring the average number of extensions observed over a 10-min window for each embryo (Fig. 2D) and by measuring the maximum length of each extension (Fig. 2E). Analyses were conducted in a blinded manner, with image acquisition and data quantification performed before receiving genotyping results. Consistent with the hypothesized role of CDON in ventral neural tube cytoneme formation, removal of one copy of Cdon reduced the average number and length of cytonemes independent of Boc status (Fig. 2, D and E, column 1 versus columns 2 and 3). Deletion of both copies of Cdon further reduced cytoneme numbers but did not lead to additional length reductions of extensions that did form (Fig. 2, D and E, columns 4 and 5).

SHH from the notochord and floor plate controls fate determination in ventral cell populations of the neural tube. The duration and concentration of SHH exposure dictate which transcriptional programs are activated, making specific transcription factors reliable markers for each cell population. These include, in a ventral to dorsal trajectory, FOXA2 in ventral-most cells of the floor plate, the high signal threshold target NKX2.2, intermediate ventral target OLIG2, PAX6 in the intermediate zone abutting the dorsal compartment, and PAX7 marking dorsal intermediate cell populations (56, 57). Cross-repressive activities by these transcription factors ensure that each marker is restricted to the appropriate cell population (58). As such, analysis of the position and size of each marked cell population allows for direct reporting of SHH signaling gradient activity. To determine whether reduced cytoneme numbers and lengths resulting from Cdon deletion correlated with altered SHH gradient function, we sectioned E9.5 (∼25 somite) Shh-Cre;Boc+/−;Cdonfl/fl and Shh-Cre;Boc−/−;Cdonfl/fl embryos to quantify progenitor domain areas. Boc+/−;Cdonfl/fl lacking a Cre driver served as a control.

Notochord-derived SHH induces the FOXA2-positive floor plate, which functions as a secondary source of SHH protein for neural tube patterning (59). Suggestive of a role for notochord-derived CDON in deploying SHH to the floor plate, we observed a significant reduction in floor plate size relative to overall neural tube area in E9.5 Shh-Cre;Boc+/−;Cdonfl/fl and Shh-Cre;Boc−/−;Cdonfl/fl embryos when compared to the controls (Fig. 3, A and B, and fig. S2F). The NKX2.2 population, which requires high SHH pathway activity for its induction, showed a similarly reduced domain area compared to controls (Fig. 3, A, middle, and B, and fig. S2F). Whereas we did not observe the overall OLIG2 domain area to be significantly reduced compared to the controls, the neighboring PAX6 progenitor population was significantly expanded (Fig. 3, A and B, and fig. S2F). This is suggestive of reduced low-level SHH signaling activity in cells further from the ligand source (58, 60). We attribute these changes to reduction in CDON activity in Shh-expressing cells, and not to loss of BOC in signal-receiving cells, because a similar PAX6 expansion is evident in Shh-Cre;Boc+/−;Cdonfl/fl embryos (Fig. 3B and fig. S2F) and Boc−/− neural tubes are phenotypically normal at E9.5 and E10.5 (51, 52).

Relative size alterations for each of these neuroprogenitor populations remained consistent at E10.5 despite neural tubes being significantly smaller than control at this developmental stage (Fig. 3, D to F). Neural tube sizes were quantified for three somite-matched Boc+/−;Cdonfl/fl and Shh-Cre;Boc−/−;Cdonfl/fl embryo pairs, revealing reduced neural tube areas and circumferences in the Cdon-deleted mutants (Fig. 3F). Measurements of the dorsoventral (DV) and apicobasal (AB) axes demonstrated a marked reduction in DV growth, likely due to attenuated SHH signaling (Fig. 3F), which promotes proliferation and suppresses apoptosis along the DV axis (61, 62). Nevertheless, the overall size of the embryos was comparable between control and Cdon-deleted animals, suggesting that the observed changes were likely specific to neural tube patterning defects and not a result of significantly delayed developmental timing in Cre-expressing embryos (Fig. 3G). Furthermore, the smaller mutant floor plates continued to express comparable levels of Shh transcript at E10.5 (Fig. 3H), supporting that the phenotypes observed were not due to impaired SHH production. Altogether, the observed alteration of high- and low-threshold SHH target gene expression suggests increased steepness of the signaling gradient following CDON protein reduction in notochord and floor plate cells. Combined with results presented above showing reduced numbers and lengths of neural tube cytonemes in Cdon conditionally deleted embryos, we conclude that disruption of the SHH signaling gradient likely results from reduced cytoneme-mediated SHH deployment from notochord and floor plate cells.

BOC and CDON intracellular domains are required for cytoneme regulation
Having identified BOC and CDON as specific regulators of SHH cytoneme formation, we next sought to determine the molecular mechanisms by which they signal to influence cytoneme behavior. Both proteins contain extracellular Ig and FNIII domains that have the potential to facilitate intermolecular interactions in cis and trans (63, 64). Accordingly, the Drosophila ortholog of CDON, Ihog, confers stability to cytonemes in wing imaginal discs through homophilic interactions (32, 33). BOC and CDON also contain intracellular domains that facilitate communication with downstream actin regulatory effectors like Bnip-2, Cdc42, and members of MAPK and JNK pathways (65–67).

We chose to focus primarily on CDON because its expression in SHH-producing cells of the developing neural tube and the effects of its deletion in this population suggest a specific role in ligand delivery (37, 49) (Figs. 2 and 3 and fig. S2). To test the requirement of CDON functional domains for cytoneme behavior, we generated deletion mutants lacking each domain. We engineered CDON proteins lacking the Ig domains (∆Ig), FNIII domains (∆FN), transmembrane domain (∆TM), or intracellular domain (∆ICD) and then tested for functional maturation and cell surface localization of each truncation mutant by analyzing N-linked glycosylation status and testing cell surface biotinylation (Fig. 4A and fig. S3, A to C). Cell surface biotinylation experiments showed that all truncation mutants, except for ∆TM, reached the cell surface (fig. S3A, lanes 6 to 8 and 10 versus lane 9). Accordingly, ∆Ig, ∆FN, and ∆ICD proteins all harbored complex N-linked glycans, as indicated by sensitivity to peptide-N-glycosidase F (PNGase), which cleaves both simple and complex N-glycan additions, and resistance to Endoglycosidase H (EndoH), which cleaves simple glycans that are present on ER-localized proteins (fig. S3, B and C). CDON∆Ig demonstrated modest mobility shifts in SDS-PAGE gels following EndoH versus PNGase treatments indicative of reduced glycosylation at baseline. This is likely due to deletion of multiple predicted N-linked glycosylation sites in the Ig domains (fig. S3, B and C, lanes 6 to 10). Consistent with its failure to reach the cell surface, ∆TM lacked EndoH-resistant complex glycans and immunofluorescence analysis of CDON∆TM-GFP-expressing Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs showed subcellular localization suggestive of ER retention (fig. S3C, lanes 16 to 20, and Fig. 4B).

To survey the effects of CDON functional domain deletion on cytoneme dynamics, we expressed each protein in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− TKO MEFs stably expressing MSCV-Hygro-SHH-FL (26, 51) and then quantified cytoneme occurrence rates (Fig. 4, B and C). Whereas ∆Ig and ∆FN CDON proteins rescued cytoneme occurrence similarly to WT CDON, ∆TM and ∆ICD did not. The inability of CDON∆TM to rescue occurrence likely stems from its inability to effectively traffic out of the ER. As such, the cytoneme regulatory signal is likely communicated to downstream effectors through the CDON ICD.

To test whether the ICD is sufficient to promote cytoneme occurrence when localized to the plasma membrane, we generated a construct lacking the ECD, CDON∆ECD-GFP, and a chimeric protein where the CDON ECD was replaced by the ECD of CD4, a transmembrane protein with four tandem Ig domains (CD4::CDON) (fig. S4A). In an effort to achieve subcellular localization similar to WT CDON, we designed the two ECD mutant constructs to retain both the signal sequence and the FN-TM linker of WT CDON. Cell surface biotinylation experiments indicated that both ECD mutants reached the cell surface; however, CDON∆ECD was present on the surface at reduced levels as indicated by lower biotinylation signal (fig. S4B, lane 6 compared to lanes 4 and 5). PNGase and EndoH sensitivity assays revealed that WT CDON and CD4::CDON exhibited complex N-linked glycosylation (fig. S4C). CDON∆ECD was unaltered by EndoH or PNGase treatment (fig. S4C), consistent with removal of all predicted N-linked glycosylation sites in the Ig and FNIII domains (figs. S4C and S3B).

Having confirmed expression and plasma membrane localization of the CDON derivatives, we next assessed whether the mutant proteins localized to cytonemes or influenced their occurrence in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs. We found that CD4::CDON entered extensions like WT CDON and increased their occurrence over baseline, albeit to a lesser intensity than the WT protein (fig. S4D). This partial rescue was similar to what was observed with CDON∆Ig and CDON∆FN and suggests that most cytoneme-promoting activity can be conferred through the ICD if it can enter the specialized filopodia (Fig. 4C and fig. S4D). Accordingly, CDON∆ECD failed to localize as efficiently to cytonemes and showed a modest increase in cytoneme occurrence over baseline (fig. S4D). Altogether, these results suggest that enrichment in cytonemes is necessary for the ICD to signal for their elongation or occurrence. The intermediate cytoneme phenotype of CD4::CDON-GFP suggests that the CDON ECD contributes to promoting cytoneme occurrence.

Like CDON, BOC re-expression can rescue SHH-induced cytoneme stimulation in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs (26). Thus, we tested whether BOC also signals to influence cytoneme behavior through its ICD. We generated BOC∆ICD-GFP, confirmed its cell surface localization and N-linked glycosylation status, and then tested its ability to promote cytoneme occurrence (fig. S5, A to E). Like what was observed for CDON, WT BOC was able to rescue SHH-stimulated cytoneme occurrence in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs, but BOC∆ICD was not (fig. S5, D and E). Together with the results presented above, this suggests that the ICDs of BOC and CDON transduce a cytoneme-promoting signal.

The CDON ICD facilitates DISP interaction
Structure/function analyses indicate that the SHH receptor PTCH associates with BOC/CDON through binding of its first large extracellular loop to BOC/CDON extracellular FNIII domains (35, 36). Given that PTCH and the SDC member DISP are structurally related (40, 41), we hypothesized that CDON binding to DISP in the SDC would occur through its ECDs. To test this, we coexpressed DISP with the CDON deletion mutants described above in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells and then performed coimmunoprecipitation analysis (Fig. 4D). Consistent with our previous report (26), GFP-tagged, full-length CDON specifically coimmunoprecipitated with V5-DISP-HA (Fig. 4D, IP lane 8 compared to lane 6). ∆Ig, ∆FN, ∆TM, and ∆ICD CDON-GFP deletion mutants were also found to coimmunoprecipitate with V5-DISP-HA, suggesting the presence of multiple binding interfaces (Fig. 4D, IP lanes 10, 12, 14, and 16). However, ∆TM and ∆ICD CDON proteins coimmunoprecipitated with V5-DISP-HA with reduced efficiency (Fig. 4D, lanes 14 and 16, top), suggesting that the ICD is likely a preferred interaction domain. We speculate that modest amount of ΔTM coimmunoprecipitating with V5-DISP-HA was likely due to failure of this truncation mutant to reach the cell surface (Fig. 4B and fig. S3A, lane 9).

To evaluate CDON/DISP interaction in cells, we performed Golgi re-colocalization assays (GRAs) (68). A C-terminal Golgi localization sequence (GLS) was fused to WT and each of the CDON-FLAG deletion mutants to tether them to the Golgi membrane (fig. S5F). V5-DISP-HA was expressed alongside these mutants in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs and re-colocalization of WT DISP to the Golgi was monitored as an in-cell reporter of CDON-DISP association (Fig. 4E). Whereas robust Golgi localization of DISP was observed with WT CDON, ΔIg, and ΔFN CDON-GLS proteins, CDONΔICD-GLS failed to concentrate DISP at the Golgi (Fig. 4E, columns 1 to 8 versus columns 9 and 10). CDONΔICD-GLS was the only CDON variant to show reduced Pearson’s correlation coefficients with V5-DISP-HA when compared to the non-GLS control (Fig. 4E, column 9 versus column 10). We did not observe a significant change in colocalization between CDON∆TM and DISP, likely due to the inability of this mutant to effectively traffic from the ER (Fig. 4E, columns 7 and 8). Altogether, these results indicate that the ICD drives stable DISP-CDON association in cells.

CDON and BOC recruit FARP1 to enable cytoneme occurrence
Because DISP cannot signal to influence cytoneme dynamics without BOC or CDON (26) (Fig. 1), we hypothesized that their ICDs bind actin regulatory effectors in addition to binding DISP. To test this in an unbiased manner, we generated BOC and CDON fusion proteins harboring a C-terminal intracellular FLAG tag followed by the BirA/TurboID biotin ligase (69) (fig. S6A). Unfortunately, the chimeric CDON-TurboID protein expressed poorly in cells, leading to insufficient biotinylation activity (fig. S6B, lane 4, control versus lanes 7 and 8, SAV). Thus, we conducted proximity labeling using BOC-TurboID. BOC-TurboID trafficked to the plasma membrane and harbored complex N-linked glycans comparable to the FLAG-tagged protein (fig. S6, C and D). To ensure that TurboID would not hinder functional interactions required for the cytoneme-promoting activity of BOC, we tested the ability of TurboID-containing BOC protein to rescue SHH cytoneme occurrence in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs. The TurboID-tagged construct rescued SHH cytoneme occurrence comparable to the FLAG-tagged construct lacking the biotin ligase (fig. S6E). The chimeric protein was able to effectively biotinylate cellular proteins, as indicated by staining with fluorescently conjugated streptavidin (fig. S6E, SAV/cyan). Altogether, these assays support feasibility of using the chimeric BOC-FLAG-TurboID protein for proteomic experimentation (fig. S6, C to E).

In addition to its role in the SDC, BOC is important for clustering SHH on receiving cells for transfer to PTCH1 (35, 36, 70). BOC is also suggested to bind PTCH2 in some contexts, and PTCH2 can compensate for PTCH1 loss in the chick neural tube, raising the possibility that the presence of PTCH1/2 receptors could bias BOC away from SDC effectors (71–73). Thus, we generated Boc/Cdon/Disp1/Ptch1/Ptch2/Smo−/− [pan receptor knockout (PRK)] MEFs to serve as a “clean” background for binding studies (fig. S1A). PRK cells were validated through loss of targeted gene transcripts, loss of induction of the SHH target Gli1, and inability to detect ligand-stimulated enrichment of the SHH signal transducing protein SMO in the primary cilium, a sensory organelle from which it signals (fig. S1, D to G). PRK cells were then transfected with TurboID or BOC-TurboID with or without SDC partners V5-DISP-HA and SHH. The cells were exposed to vehicle or biotin, and then biotinylated proteins were isolated from lysates on streptavidin-conjugated beads. Bound proteins were identified through LC-MS/MS using spectral counting-based quantification (fig. S6, F and G). We obtained high spectral counts for the coexpressed SDC components DISP and SHH, supporting that BOC-TurboID biotinylates known interaction partners (fig. S6G).

Given our hypothesis that the SDC communicates with cytoskeletal regulators to promote cytoneme initiation and/or elongation, we searched the dataset for direct actin regulators. We observed enrichment of members of the WAVE regulatory complex (fig. S6G), which is consistent with a recent report on BOC’s interaction with this complex in Rac1-driven actin polymerization for SHH-mediated axon guidance (74). To find potential cytoneme-promoting signaling molecules, we looked for Rho GTPases, which specifically alter actin dynamics at the plasma membrane (75). Although BOC proximity labeling did not enrich specific Rho GTPases, it did modestly enrich Rho activating GEFs (fig. S6G). We selected dedicator of cytokinesis 7 (DOCK7) and FARP1 for further analysis because of their established connections to actin regulation (76–78). We also included intersectin-1 (ITSN1), despite it showing low spectral counts in the BOC-TurboID dataset, because the intracellular domains of both BOC and CDON have polyproline motifs that can function as putative ITSN1 binding sites per Scansite 4.0 (79) (fig. S6H).

To test whether any of the candidate BOC interactors localize to cytonemes, we expressed DOCK7-GFP, FARP1-GFP, and ITSN1-mCherry in NIH3T3 cells and examined their subcellular localization. FARP1 was the only GEF that was detected in cytonemes, and it appeared to concentrate at cytoneme tips in SHH-expressing cells (Fig. 5A). Accordingly, FARP1-GFP was the only GEF that, when overexpressed in the absence of SHH, elevated baseline cytoneme occurrence rates (Fig. 5B). Whereas DOCK7-GFP had no impact on cytoneme occurrence rates, ITSN1-mCherry blocked the ability of SHH to increase cytoneme dynamics as compared to control (Fig. 5B). We speculate that ITSN1 overexpression may reduce SDC cell surface occupancy to prevent cytoneme biogenesis due to its ability to enable clathrin-mediated endocytosis (80–82). This is because DISP/SHH internalization occurs through clathrin-mediated endocytosis and both BOC and PTCH are internalized in an SHH-dependent manner through the clathrin adaptor Numb (10, 83, 84). As such, ITSN1, which directly interacts with Numb in neurogenesis (85), might serve as a general facilitator of SHH receptor endocytosis following ligand binding.

Given our observation that CDON promotes cytoneme occurrence in SHH-producing cells of the developing neural tube, we were keen to test whether CDON might interact with FARP1 in cells. Thus, we performed a proximity ligation assay (PLA) in NIH3T3 cells expressing CDON-FLAG and FARP1-GFP. We observed PLA signal between the two proteins along cytoneme lengths in both the absence and presence of SHH, and noted increased intensity of the PLA signal near cytoneme tips when SHH was coexpressed (fig. S7A), As a negative control, we tested for PLA activity between CDON-FLAG and a GFP-tagged, truncated GLI2 transcription factor construct that accumulates in the cytoplasm. GLI2-CDON-FLAG PLA signal was modest and rarely found within the CDON/SHH-induced extensions, supporting specificity of the CDON-FARP1 PLA interaction signal in cytonemes (fig. S7A).

To evaluate subcellular localization of endogenous FARP1, we immunostained NIH3T3 cells using anti-FARP1 and observed bright FARP1 puncta localized to cytoneme-like projections (Fig. 5C, yellow arrowheads). To test specificity of this signal, cells were transfected with scrambled or Farp1 siRNA before immunostaining (Fig. 5, C and D). Whereas low-level background cytoplasmic staining was unaffected by Farp1 knockdown, the bright puncta present on cellular extensions were lost, supporting specificity of the FARP1 cytoneme signal (Fig. 5C).

To determine whether endogenous FARP1 enriched with SHH, CDON, or DISP in cytonemes, SHH-mCherry, CDON-GFP, or V5-DISP-HA was expressed in NIH3T3 cells, and each protein was visualized along with FARP1. Endogenous FARP1-positive puncta were observed in SHH-mCherry, CDON-GFP, or V5-DISP-HA-positive cytonemes (Fig. 5E, yellow arrowheads), suggesting a functional contribution to cytoneme-based SDC activity. To test whether FARP1 is required for SHH cytoneme formation, we knocked down Farp1 in NIH3T3 cells expressing SHH-mCherry and quantified cytoneme occurrence rates. SHH could not increase cytoneme occurrence over baseline following FARP1 knockdown, suggesting that the GEF is an essential downstream signaling effector of SDC regulation of cytoneme biogenesis or elongation (Fig. 5F).

Cdc42 activation downstream of the SDC increases SHH cytoneme occurrence
FARP1 is a member of the Dbl GEF family that has been linked to dendritic spine formation and synaptogenesis in neurons (77, 78, 86, 87). As a Dbl GEF, FARP1 structure includes tandem Dbl-Homology (DH) and pleckstrin homology (PH) domains, crucial for membrane targeting and substrate binding (88) (fig. S7B). FARP1 activity toward the Rho GTPases RhoA, Rac1, and Cdc42 is context dependent (77, 78, 89–91), necessitating empirical evaluation of which GTPase functions downstream of the GEF to influence cytoneme dynamics. Thus, we obtained constitutively active (CA), GFP-tagged RhoA, Rac1, and Cdc42 constructs, and then expressed each GTPase in NIH3T3 cells alone or with SHH-mCherry to evaluate the impact on cytoneme occurrence (Fig. 6, A and B). Only CA Cdc42 boosted baseline cytoneme occurrence rates. CA RhoA was not significantly different from the control cells, and, like ITSN1, CA Rac1 blunted the ability of SHH to induce cytonemes (Fig. 6B). CA Rac1 expression stimulated lamellipodia formation (Fig. 6A), suggestive of activation of effectors that oppose filopodial extension and instead promote assembly of branched actin ruffles through WAVE complex activity (92, 93). These results suggest that Cdc42 may be activated downstream of BOC/CDON-FARP1 signaling to promote cytonemes. To test whether Cdc42 is required for SHH-stimulated cytoneme biogenesis, we transfected NIH3T3 cells with either mCherry or SHH-mCherry and then treated cells with either dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or the specific Cdc42 inhibitor ML141 (94). Cytoneme occurrence rates were scored 1 hour after drug treatment. Suggestive of Cdc42 signaling downstream of SHH for cytoneme initiation, ML141 treatment eliminated the SHH effect on cytoneme occurrence rates (Fig. 6C).

If Cdc42 is a downstream SDC effector that promotes cytoneme formation or elongation, we hypothesized that it is likely recruited to sites of cytoneme outgrowth in a transient manner by CDON or BOC. Thus, we tested whether CDON can recruit Cdc42 to specific subcellular localizations using the GRA as described above. Consistent with CDON being a Cdc42 recruiter, we found that Golgi-localized CDON-GLS relocalized Cdc42-GFP from the cell body to the Golgi (Fig. 6D). Relocalization occurred similarly in both the absence and presence of SHH, suggesting that CDON-mediated Cdc42 recruitment is not ligand dependent (Fig. 6D). Rac1-GFP, which did not influence cytoneme dynamics, was not recruited to the Golgi by CDON-GLS and showed reduced Pearson’s colocalization coefficient values following CDON Golgi tethering (Fig. 6E). These results, along with the results presented above, allowed us to conclude that the SDC components BOC or CDON recruit the GEF FARP1 and its substrate Cdc42 to regulate actin dynamics for cytoneme outgrowth.

Cdc42 activity in SHH cytonemes requires BOC/CDON
Having identified Cdc42 as the putative GTPase acting downstream of the SDC in cytonemes, we next sought to visualize endogenous Cdc42 activity in the extensions using a Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET)–based Cdc42 biosensor (95). A limitation to FRET efficiency analysis is fluorescence intensity–based variation across conditions and samples, which could be exacerbated in thin cytonemes (96). To avoid this potential complication, we adapted a fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM)–FRET protocol for quantitative analysis of Cdc42 activity in cell bodies and cytonemes (96). We transfected the biosensor into NIH3T3 cells stably expressing SHH-FL and performed live imaging to capture dynamic Cdc42 activity over time (Fig. 7A, fig. S8A, and movie S5). Observation of a singular extension/retraction event demonstrated high Cdc42 activity at the tip during elongation, which was subsequently lost before its retraction toward the cell body (fig. S8A). This behavior is consistent with expected Cdc42 activation dynamics in filopodial-like structures and with the observed colocalization of CDON and FARP1 at cytoneme tips in PLAs, validating that this biosensor is suitable for Cdc42 activity measurements.

To quantify activity in distinct subcellular domains, regions of interest (ROIs) including the whole cell (WC), ∼5 μm of the cell periphery (Per), the central node (CN), and individual cellular extensions (Ind Ext) were analyzed (Fig. 7A and fig. S8B). For statistical analysis, individual extension FLIM-FRET efficiency values were averaged to provide a single value per cell for cells that had multiple extensions (Ext Avg versus Ind Ext) (fig. S8B). Because each cell expressed varying baseline Cdc42 biosensor activity, we calculated FLIM-FRET efficiency fold change between ROIs within the same cell to directly compare relative localized Cdc42 activity across multiple cells and experiments (Fig. 7A and fig. S8C). For these assays, significance was calculated against a fold change of 1.00 (Fig. 7A and fig. S8C, blue significance indicators).

Cdc42 activity was elevated at the cell periphery compared to the whole cell or central node (Fig. 7A, Per/WC column 1 and Per/CN column 4, black dots, and fig. S8B). This result was anticipated because Cdc42 requires membrane localization for its activation (95, 97). Consistent with a role for Cdc42 in SHH cytonemes, the highest levels of endogenous GTPase activity were detected in cytoneme-like extensions (Fig. 7A, Ext Avg/WC column 3, black dots, and fig. S8, B and C), even when compared to the cell periphery (Fig. 7A, Ext Avg/Per column 5, black dots, and fig. S8, B and C).

To quantify the magnitude of elevated Cdc42 activity in the extensions, the FLIM-FRET efficiency values for each cell were plotted starting from the central node through the periphery and ultimately to the extension averages (fig. S8B, black solid lines). Least squares regression fits were calculated for each individual cell, resulting in a large average slope value (3195, R2 = 0.9139), indicating elevated activity in the extensions compared to the other ROIs (fig. S8B, dotted red lines).

To confirm specificity of the active Cdc42 signal, we treated sensor-expressing cells with the Cdc42 inhibitor ML141. ML141 treatment reduced activity of the biosensor, resulting in FLIM-FRET efficiency ratios near baseline and a moderate regression slope from central node to periphery and extensions (589.8, R2 = 0.9501) (Fig. 7A and fig. S8C, red dots compared to black dots, black asterisks; fig. S8D). On the basis of these results, we conclude that Cdc42 is active in cytonemes of SHH-expressing NIH3T3 cells.

Last, to test whether cytoneme-localized Cdc42 activity in SHH-expressing cells is associated with BOC and/or CDON function, we evaluated biosensor FLIM-FRET efficiency in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs, in which baseline and WNT1-stimulated cytoneme occurrence rates are unchanged and SHH-stimulated cytoneme biogenesis is compromised (26) (fig. S2C). Consistent with the inability of SHH to enhance cytoneme occurrence in cells lacking SDC activity, endogenous Cdc42 activity was only modestly enhanced in the Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− + SHH MEF extensions, resulting in a reduced value for slope from central node through periphery to extensions (1625, R2 = 0.9223) (fig. S8E). Accordingly, Ext/WC and Ext/Per ratios were decreased (Fig. 7B, columns 3 and 5, black dots; fig. S8F; and movie S6) and ML141 inhibition of Per/WC, Ext/WC, and Ext/Per Cdc42 activity ratios was lost in Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− cells (Fig. 7B and fig. S8F, red dots compared to black). The ROI regression slope decreased slightly with ML141 treatment (1345, R2 = 0.8361) (fig. S8G). However, FLIM-FRET efficiency remained comparable to vehicle-treated cells (fig. S8G), suggesting that in the absence of BOC and CDON, Cdc42 activity in cellular extensions of SHH-expressing cells is compromised. Altogether, these results provide supportive evidence that the SDC components BOC and CDON enable localized FARP1-mediated Cdc42 activation for outgrowth of SHH-containing cytonemes in ligand-producing cells (Fig. 7C).

DISCUSSION
A growing body of evidence supports the idea that cytonemes are key contributors to regulated deployment and reception of intercellular signals during development and tissue homeostasis. They transport morphogens, growth factors, and receptors, and their activity directly promotes signal gradient formation and precision across developing tissues (10, 17–19, 24, 31, 98, 99). Consistent with cytonemes being actin-based structures, their elongation and function are reliant upon actin regulatory proteins (8, 18, 27, 28, 31, 100). Herein, we demonstrate that, in the case of SHH cytoneme-based transport, BOC and CDON promote activation of the actin regulatory Rho GTPase Cdc42 by recruiting its GEF FARP1. Live imaging of cultured cells reveals that loss of BOC and CDON blunts SHH-stimulated Cdc42 activity in cytonemes, supporting that BOC and CDON confer signaling competence to the SDC for actin control. Live imaging of E9.5 neural tube sections supports that this functionality is conserved in vivo. Deletion of Cdon specifically in SHH-producing neuroepithelial cells reduces dynamic cytoneme behavior, occurrence frequency, and length, which correlates with altered ventral cell fate establishment in the developing neural tube. Altogether, these results support a model in which CDON and BOC can function as signaling competent deployment receptors that recruit FARP1 and Cdc42 to instruct actin polymerization for cytoneme elongation and SHH transport (Fig. 7C, left).

Loading of SHH into nascent cytonemes is proposed to occur through entry of SDC-containing vesicles into and along the signaling filopodia through the action of cytoneme-localized MYO10 (10, 26). BOC or CDON-FARP1 signaling from cytoneme membrane and SDC-containing vesicles then ensures continued actin polymerization for cytoneme elongation toward target cells (Fig. 7C, right). Thus, SHH binding proteins of the SDC likely promote ligand transport through linking parallel pathways of (i) DISP-mediated SHH vesicle packaging and (ii) BOC/CDON-mediated cytoneme outgrowth. Whereas DISP is not required for cytoneme elongation, its binding to BOC/CDON spatially couples extension outgrowth with SHH deployment machinery to ensure efficient ligand transport.

BOC and CDON were first identified as founding members of a subfamily of immunoglobulin and fibronectin domain-containing CAM-like proteins that promote myogenesis during skeletal muscle development (63, 64). In this context, CDON signaling leads to activation of Cdc42, which signals to p38/MAPK for muscle differentiation. However, in muscle, Cdc42 recruitment occurs following CDON ligation to N-cadherin, which promotes CDON association with the Cdc42-binding protein Bnip-2 (65, 66, 101).

Notably, SHH-bound CDON does not associate with Bnip-2 (101). Accordingly, BOC and CDON contributions to SHH signaling were initially attributed to them functioning as SHH co-receptors and not to their ability to communicate with actin regulators. Their function in the pathway was thought to be restricted to SHH-receiving cells, where they cooperate with PTCH to enhance SHH signaling during neuronal cell fate specification and axon guidance (36, 37, 83, 102). However, PTCH does not require BOC/CDON function for SHH binding (40). Moreover, Boc−/− neural tubes are phenotypically normal at the embryonic stages when progenitor domain establishment occurs, and Boc−/− mice are viable without overt Hedgehog phenotypes (51, 52). As such, BOC and CDON were proposed to function in the pathway primarily to extend the range of SHH responsiveness to low levels of ligand exposure (37). The precise role of CDON in the notochord, which produces SHH but does not respond to it, was not initially clear.

Recent investigations into cytoneme biology provide insight into functions of the co-receptors in signal-producing cells, revealing roles for BOC/CDON and the Drosophila CDON ortholog Ihog in cytoneme-based SHH/Hh transport (14, 26, 30, 33, 34, 103). Like their roles in ligand-receiving cells, cytoneme-specific activity of BOC/CDON in signal-producing cells was initially attributed to activities of their ECDs. Studies in chick limb buds showed BOC and CDON enrichment at cytoneme contact points and, in Drosophila, Ihog forms cytoneme-cytoneme connections by associating in trans (14, 32). Ihog can also bind extracellular matrix components to stabilize cytoneme extensions (17, 32, 33, 103).

The results presented here suggest that most BOC/CDON cytoneme-promoting activity occurs through their ICDs, which recruit the actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42. However, CDON mutants lacking an intact ECD cannot promote cytonemes as effectively as the WT protein, suggesting that some cytoneme-promoting activity occurs extracellularly. We speculate that, like the Ihog ECD, the BOC and CDON ECDs could provide adhesion functionality that stabilizes elongated cytonemes, either through homophilic interactions in trans or through binding extracellular interaction partners. Notably, BOC and CDON interact in cis with N-cadherin and M-cadherin at myoblast cell-cell contact sites (104), and CDON coordinates N-cadherin positioning at the cell surface for directed neural crest cell migration in zebrafish (50). Thus, precedent exists for indirect roles for BOC and CDON in cell-cell adhesion. The contribution of such interactions in a cytoneme context warrants further investigation.

The first direct evidence for BOC or CDON initiating a cellular signal downstream of SHH was revealed through interrogation of BOC function in growth cones of commissural axons. Here, SHH binding to BOC leads to SMO-independent mobilization of the GEFs DOCK3/4, which activate Rac1 for cytoskeletal reorganization (105). This observation, combined with the data presented here that both proteins appear to signal in cytonemes for actin regulation, suggests that BOC or CDON recruitment of FARP1 may represent cytoneme-specific signal customization. Notably, FARP1 activity is linked to formation of filopodia and another type of signaling protrusion, the tunneling nanotube (TNT) (77, 90, 106). Like what is shown here for cytonemes, FARP1-mediated promotion of TNTs requires Cdc42 (90). This suggests that Cdc42 recruitment may be a broadly used mechanism by which specialized signaling protrusions are controlled.

Consistent with a conserved role for Cdc42 in cytoneme elongation, in vivo studies demonstrate that its activity is necessary for outgrowth of both WNT8a and NOTCH containing cytonemes. Knockdown of Cdc42a/c in zebrafish leads to reduction in numbers and lengths of WNT8a-positive cytonemes, and ML141-mediated Cdc42 inhibition in spinal cord explants reduces cytoneme density across NOTCH-responsive cell populations (18, 28). However, Cdc42-independent cytoneme transport can occur. Cytonemes containing FGFR are dependent on the atypical Rho GTPase RhoD, which signals through mDia3C to stimulate actin polymerization for cytoneme elongation (27). Whether this suggests customized engagement of different GEFs/GTPases by distinct signaling pathways or highlights a difference between ligand versus receptor-transporting protrusions is not yet known. However, it is notable that, like BOC and CDON, FGFR contains tandem Ig domains that are essential for its function (107). ROR2, which promotes WNT5b and WNT8a cytoneme biogenesis, also harbors Ig domains (11, 29, 108), suggesting that cargo binding to Ig-containing, adhesion-related molecules may promote cytoneme-based transport.

With respect to both function and regulation, cytonemes appear to share several characteristics with neurons (109). Glutamatergic signaling promotes cytoneme formation and stability, and a recent study on WNT7a-containing cytonemes suggests that the signaling protrusions are characteristically similar to dendritic filopodia (16, 20, 110, 111). Notably, FARP1 has been demonstrated to promote dynamic behavior of dendritic filopodia in immature neurons and to stimulate formation of vGLUT1/2-positive presynaptic sites in differentiated neurons (77, 78). We propose that BOC and/or CDON recruitment of FARP1 to the SDC redirects FARP1 activity toward cytoneme elongation, highlighting another similarity between neuronal extensions and the specialized signaling filopodia.

Despite their complementary expression domains in the developing neural tube spanning SHH, WNT, and BMP signaling zones, our data suggest that BOC and CDON contributions to cytoneme-mediated signaling may be specific to SHH. Boc/Cdon/Gas1−/− MEFs do not show reduced WNT-stimulated cytoneme occurrence rates in vitro. Moreover, the PAX7 expression domain, which is specified by cytoneme cargoes WNT and FGF, does not show overt changes in Shh-Cre;Boc−/−;Cdonfl/fl neural tubes (8, 112, 113). By contrast, functional loss of the actin motor MYO10 disrupts both ventral SHH activity and dorsal WNT activity in the neural tube, consistent with a broadly used cytoneme function (10).

Given that both BOC and CDON can induce cytonemes in cultured cells, and that their cytoneme-promoting activity appears to be specific to SHH, it is tempting to speculate that the split expression domains of Boc and Cdon in the developing neural tube may directly shape SHH signaling gradient length by promoting cytoneme formation from both signal-sending and -receiving cells. In this scenario, CDON is proposed to function in signal-producing cells of the notochord and floor plate to stimulate extension of dorsally projecting cytonemes for SHH delivery. BOC would then function in signal-receiving cells to induce ventrally projecting cytonemes that synapse with floor plate–derived extensions for ligand delivery along the entire length of the SHH signaling gradient. The proposed activity is supported by studies of the Drosophila wing disc that demonstrate that Ptc-containing cytonemes extend from Hh-receiving cells to directly receive ligand from Ihog-induced, signal-sending cytonemes (31). Thus, BOC expression in ligand-responding tissue of the neural tube may facilitate dual roles in both cytoneme extension and pathway activation. Clustering of BOC at the plasma membrane through its interaction with PTCH is hypothesized to drive both of these functions.

The proposed model does not exclude the possibility that BOC and CDON could also function in diffusion-based SHH reception. We hypothesize that their activity can be shaped by their subcellular localization such that BOC/CDON localization to cytonemes and/or binding to the SDC promotes communication with actin, and their enrichment on cellular membranes near GAS1 directs them to receive diffusible SHH/SCUBE2 complexes. Consistent with this hypothesis, a recent non–peer-reviewed preprint suggests that Ihog directly binds the Drosophila functional ortholog of SCUBE2, Shifted (Shf), to solubilize Hh at cytoneme contact sites (114).

The ability of both BOC and CDON to influence cytoskeletal rearrangements in context-dependent manners highlights how functional repurposing of protein activity can be used to customize cellular signaling behavior. The results presented here demonstrate how such customization can ensure proper distribution of SHH from signaling centers like the notochord and floor plate to target cell populations during neuroepithelial cell fate determination. We hypothesize that similar strategies are applied by other signals and receptors transported by cytonemes and suggest that studies aimed at identifying pathway-specific modes of recruiting actin regulators will help to define how signal precision is maintained in dynamic tissue environments.

Plasmid transfection
Cells were seeded at 60 to 80% confluency a day before transfection. Plasmids were transfected using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Cells were fixed and/or lysed for analysis ∼24 to 48 hours following transfection.

siRNA transfection
Cells were reverse transfected using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, 5 μl of RNAiMAX was diluted with either 30 pmol medium GC siScr (Invitrogen 462001) or 10 pmol each of three siFarp1 Silencer Select siRNAs (Invitrogen 4390771: s104494, s104495, and s104496) in 1 ml of Optimum in 6-well plates and incubated rocking at room temperature (RT) for 10 min. NIH3T3 cells were added in 1 ml of cDMEM at 50% confluency and incubated overnight. The following day, medium was removed for subsequent transfection with plasmids.

Drug treatments
For Cdc42 inhibition, cells were treated with 10 μM ML141 (Selleck Chemicals S7686) dissolved in DMSO or DMSO vehicle in serum-free DMEM for 1 hour at 37°C before fixation as in (94).

For treatment with Smoothened Agonist (SAG), cells were seeded at 90 to 100% confluency. The next day, they were serum starved in cDMEM for 2 hours at 37°C, and then treated with DMSO vehicle or 100 nM SAG (Selleck Chemical Company) diluted in cDMEM + 0.5% FBS overnight at 37°C. Following 24 hours of SAG treatment, the cells were analyzed through qRT-PCR, immunoblotting, or immunofluorescence as described below.

Quantitative real-time PCR
Cells were seeded into 60- or 100-mm dishes and, if applicable, treated as indicated. Approximately 18 hours postseeding or treatment, total RNA was extracted using TRIzol/chloroform and isopropanol. Then, 1000 ng of RNA was converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription kit (Applied Biosystems). qRT-PCR reactions were conducted using a QuantStudio 7 Flex PCR machine using PowerUp Sybr Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems). Fold change in expression levels was calculated using the ΔΔCt method relative to the Btf3 housekeeping gene. CRISPR-edited genes were evaluated using primers designed to bind to sgRNA-targeted sequence.
